story_text.value:
Hi everyone, we love maps and doing some fun side quests exploring this domain.

We were always surprised by the fact that products like ChatGpt recommends you places to go which have been shut down for years.

Last March we built a benchmark measuring how often LLMs make mistakes when answering places-based queries (e.g. Recommend me a restaurant in Marina for a dinner). Even with the web grounding (which is a very expensive tool relative to the token price), the results were not good - 1 out 10 places in the best model were made up or shut-down.

When personal assistants started to come up, we were curious to check how well they do with those queries. It turns out that much better, but they also take longer time to answer. We make it slightly more challenging, we made a benchmark a bit more sophisticated and measured it.

The best one turned out to be Dots from OpenAI, and it is also one of the fastest. The worst one was Grok Bot from XAI. We also measured Ask Maps from Google, but it was out of competition, because it is not technically a personal assistant. The more detailed results are available in the repository

title.value: Show HN: PlaceBench – Testing AI on opening and closing hours (and last trains)

story_text.value:
As a solo-dev with a lot of projects going on, I found myself needing to make short promos or explainer videos. Not being familiar with animation software, I had the idea to use Claude to code up those videos and export them as video files. Note that this was before AI-coded music videos went viral, back in the early days when the models were just getting good enough to make the result actually look good.

In the process of creating these clips I stumbled into a bunch of bugs and setup needed to make it work reliably. The list of features I wanted for better control and feedback kept growing and I needed to sign up for a bunch of services to get music, voiceovers and other media into my project. I couldn't find an existing service that had everything I wanted. Seeing these hurdles and that the technology was only easily accessible to people already confident with coding agents, I started working on Klistra, and a couple of months later I'm turning it into a service so you all can use it too.

The goal with Klistra was to include everything I missed in the manual workflow into an easy to use service with a nice UI, so people could focus on what they wanted the video to look like, not setting up the framework behind it. Klistra includes precise timeline control, media generation, built in support to make animations match the rhythm of the background music, word extraction from voiceovers or songs, a dedicated iteration / feedback tool, web scraper and much more.

Something I knew I needed to get right was making it easy to iterate on small features of the video with precise control of what was being built. I designed Klistra so you first create a specification where you define scenes in detail, describe what you want shown and when, reference media or timestamps in-line, freely drag the timeline around and preview the result before letting a builder agent create the video. If you want to change something, the specification changes and the builder agent gets a diff of what changed. This way there is always a written specification that matches the render / build. There is also a planner agent built into Klistra that helps create and edit the specification for you (which is what I use the most), while letting you turn to manual fine-tuning when needed.

Don't think of this as a replacement for diffusion models, if you want photorealistic images or videos they clearly do a better job. Klistra really shines when you need motion design and precise control, exact text with your fonts, media such as logos or voiceovers, animated UI that matches your apps and so on. Klistra does have built in integrations for generating media from diffusion models, and combining the two technologies usually gets the best results.

Everything that costs money to run on Klistra, from machines to AI tokens, is paid for with credits included in a subscription or bought via one time packs (Pro starting at $25/mo and packs at $12). Being a solo-dev without funding, the budget wouldn't allow for a free tier with enough monthly credits for a real project. I instead decided to give the first 200 of you who sign up 350 free credits, enough for a simple video (the advanced tutorial used around 250 credits).

I created tutorials covering the basics. Mostly relying on the planner: https://klistra.ai/docs/basic and for advanced features and manual control: https://klistra.ai/docs/advanced

You can see demo videos on the home page https://klistra.ai/ and on the tutorial pages. I would love to see what you make!

Some additional notes:

- After feedback from friends there is also a Claude Code integration in paid subscriptions, where your agent can act as a planner, convenient if you already have a project built with Claude that has all the context and you need an explainer, ad or social post. It also reduces credit spending if you're a heavy planner user.

- Klistra can create images too.

Happy to hear what you think!

title.value: Show HN: Klistra – A complete studio for spec-driven AI motion design and video

story_text.value:
Hi HN, we're Shane, Sam, and Abhi.

Almost two years ago, we shared Mastra, our open-source TypeScript agent framework, on Show HN: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43103073. It got a few hundred upvotes; a couple of weeks later our downloads had doubled, and we were off to the races.

Today we're sharing Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we built to help maintain Mastra itself.

At Mastra, we now average nearly 4M downloads per week, and with Factory our team now merges hundreds of PRs a week across the mastra-ai GitHub org. Last week, Factory opened and merged 238 PRs, alongside 630 merged PRs from humans.

There's a lot of debate about what a software factory is. For us Factory is a configurable agentic kanban board that's @-taggable in Slack.

Under the hood, it uses Mastra’s durable agents for long-running sessions, our conversational memory system, a markdown based wiki with source citations to incorporate company knowledge, signals that subscribe to PR comments wired up into sessions, and a customizable cloud sandbox with our coding harness (working on supporting Claude Code, Codex etc).

When we started out, we modeled Factory around our existing workflow-oriented process (triage, plan, build, review, shipped). Three months later, we find ourselves mostly driving it through Slack vs a web UI.

We’ve seen more senior engineers kick off sessions in parallel (“triage the 20 oldest issues and let’s evaluate…”). We’re using bug and vuln scanners now, and we’ve closed our repo to outside contributors, asking folks to write detailed issue repros instead.

You can get started with `npm create factory`.

It’s fully open-source, so you can run it entirely on your infra (we also offer a hosted version). Comment here, we would love to know what you think!

https://factory.mastra.ai

https://github.com/mastra-ai/template-factory

story_text.value:
As part of our red-teaming efforts, we recently configured GPT-6 Astra to test how easily an AI agent can bypass existing bot detection and human verification systems.

We built a tool that lets you run the same test on your own website: https://assess.poh.org

Enter your website URL, and we'll launch an AI agent to test your workflows, record its actions, and show how we evaluate the session.

Below are three recorded tests. In the recorded tests below, agents were able to complete CAPTCHAs, bypass existing bot detection mechanisms, create and verify accounts, access gated resources, and carry out end-to-end workflows intended for humans.

Hugging Face: https://assess.poh.org/test/2d75a3b713e2719e87a4b85c6b3aff70 (bypassed hCAPTCHA)

Cloudflare: https://assess.poh.org/test/0eb218ca6e2d7be993b689dd69a1cb20 (bypassed Turnstile)

YouGov: https://assess.poh.org/test/144f6d014fbf006b61ec6bc32ee8c3f4 (bypassed reCAPTCHA)

AI agents are ushering in a new age of online security, and we’re excited to hear your thoughts!

title.value: Show HN: Can an AI Agent Bypass Your Website Security?

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

Dez is a free open source way to interact with AIs across providers in a full-featured text editor.

I really loved Zed's text threads feature, and after they removed it got inspired to revive it in this app.

In this latest release, Dez acts as a sandboxed agent with multimedia focused tools. It can invoke other models to generate assets and call its bundled ffmpeg to edit them.

Dez won't harm your computer, it has no way of doing so, and the ffmpeg command is sandboxed with Seatbelt on macOS and Landlock on linux.

It's also built with privacy in mind, so it's designed not to send absolute file paths to providers that might reveal things like usernames, folder names, etc.

Give it a try and let me know what you think!

title.value: Show HN: Dez – plaintext open source AI multimedia studio

story_text.value:
I've published three audio decoders under the MIT licence: FLAC, MP3, and DST (the lossless compression inside SACDs). C++17, no dependencies.

How many times faster they run than FFmpeg's own decoders:

  Desktop (i9-14900K): FLAC x2.37 faster   MP3 x2.25 faster   DST x2.01 faster
  Apple M4:            FLAC x3.45 faster   MP3 x2.76 faster   DST x2.06 faster
  Raspberry Pi 5:      FLAC x1.58 faster   MP3 x2.27 faster   DST x2.89 faster
FLAC and DST output is identical to FFmpeg's

The code is here: https://github.com/orpheic/orpheic-decoders

tools/bench.sh downloads eight freely licensed recordings from Wikimedia Commons and repeats the FLAC and MP3 comparison against the FFmpeg you have installed.

Limits: the MP3 number is for a fast path (the exact path is slower than FFmpeg).

The code was written by an AI model (Claude) under my direction, nothing was accepted without a measurement. They're the decoders inside Orpheic, a free music player I'm building.

title.value: Show HN: FLAC, MP3 and DST decoders, about 2x faster than FFmpeg's (MIT)

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I've worked with Jira Server and Data Center for years, and I'm still somewhat fond of what you could do in terms of customization.

So I built Windshift as the closest open source match to how Jira works: a single AGPL-3.0 binary, with a documented Jira Cloud and Data Center importer covering work items, custom fields, workflows, screens, sprints, etc.

It also improves on some of what Jira does. For example, you can create Configuration Sets with workflows, work item definitions, priorities and more, then apply them to several workspaces at once and import / export them without the need for 3rd party software. The UI is designed to be fast so you don't need to wait around for a view to load. There is built-in integration for Github, Gitea, ForgeJo and Gitlab already.

There are also several ways to work with AI assistance: in the product, through coding sandboxes, or via an external CLI and MCP server.

Windshift is simple to run - either as a standalone binary, rootless docker container or even packaged as a standalone mac app that can also connect to remote instances later on.

Happy to answer any questions you might have

title.value: Show HN: Windshift – the Jira alternative for people who liked Jira

story_text.value:
Hi HN! I used teams of Opus 5.5 agents to build a life-size 3D version of Treasure Island, in the middle of the San Francisco Bay. The game has 16 miles of road, almost 200 buildings, over 40 kinds of plants and over 400 drivable cars. It runs on Godot, with data from OSM, USGS lidar, and public and private photos.

I started this after moving to the island and falling in love with it. From stunning views to giant piles of dirt, pelicans to nuclear waste, this place has it all. You can explore the entire island on foot, take to the skies with a jetpack and “borrow” any car.

The native versions run best and look best, with Forward+ rendering and dynamic time of day. Web works too but the Godot WebGL 2 compatibility renderer is holding on for dear life.

I did not write the code or create the 3D models. I set up the agent teams, the working environment and the ground rules. Throughout the process I checked the output, play tested and supplied private photo data where public sources had gaps.

Trailer: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yW2SQmB-2i0 How it was built: https://grandtreasureisland.vercel.app/#how

Let me know what you think!

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I started indexed_bzip2 years ago as a seekable, parallelized bzip2 backend for ratarmount. It has been dormant for a while and seemed almost finished. Out of interest, I tried looking for bugs with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which found dozens of them, most with a minimal reproducing test. After reviewing and merging those and making a bugfix release, I prompted it with: "Speed up decompression by 2x". Surprisingly, it worked! You can try it out yourself with (timings on Ryzen 3900X):

    pip install indexed_bzip2==2.0  # Depending on your default: --uploaded-prior-to P0D, or uvx, pipx
    
    # single-threaded gzip decompression
    time igzip  -d -c      silesia-20x.tar.gz  | cksum  # 7.5 s
    time  gzip  -d -c      silesia-20x.tar.gz  | cksum  # 22.4 s
    
    # single-core bzip2
    time  bzip2 -d -c      silesia-20x.tar.bz2 | cksum  # 105 s
    time lbzip2 -d -c -n 1 silesia-20x.tar.bz2 | cksum  # 77.6 s
    time ibzip2 -d -c -P 1 silesia-20x.tar.bz2 | cksum  # 23.7 s
    
    # parallelized
    time lbzip2 -d -c      silesia-20x.tar.bz2 | cksum  # 6.7 s
    time ibzip2 -d -c      silesia-20x.tar.bz2 | cksum  # 3.8 s

    # single-threaded compression
    time  igzip -c          silesia-20x.tar    | cksum  # 11.3 s
    time   gzip -c          silesia-20x.tar    | cksum  # 147 s
    time  bzip2 -c -z       silesia-20x.tar    | cksum  # 312 s
    time ibzip2 -c -z -P 1  silesia-20x.tar    | cksum  # 164 s
    
    # parallel compression
    time lbzip2 -z -c -n 24 silesia-20x.tar    | cksum  # 12.7 s
    time ibzip2 -z -c -P 24 silesia-20x.tar    | cksum  # 13.7 s
It not only added lots of dynamically dispatched SIMD code, ABI3 wheels, Trusted Publishing, all things I had long dreaded setting up, but also found libsais for an early inverse-BWT speedup. A contributor then used Claude Fable to replace libsais with an interleaved lane-walking inverse-BWT and SIMD symbol kernels, which hides the random pointer-chase latency and gave another 1.7x. The lane interleaving follows: Karkkainen, Juha, Dominik Kempa, and Simon J. Puglisi. "Slashing the time for BWT inversion." 2012 Data Compression Conference. IEEE.

Code: https://github.com/mxmlnkn/librapidarchive/

ReadMe: https://github.com/mxmlnkn/librapidarchive/blob/HEAD/python/...

Benchmarks: https://github.com/mxmlnkn/librapidarchive/blob/HEAD/results...

story_text.value:
I run a small software agency in Germany. And of course I had some kind of software to manage my projects. It was a very simple ticket tool, and I also did my billing with it.

But one day that just annoyed me so much. I mean, you have this problem: a ticket is done. Status set to closed and you've billed it. And then two weeks later the client comes along and wants a small fix for it or a minor change, because maybe something was misunderstood. And with the tool I used, you had to put the ticket back live. But then you didn't know how many hours had already been billed, because ticket closed automatically meant ticket billed. So, and then I built my own tool. And in Lalabase it's like this: You can attach a billing to all elements, to a meeting, to a ticket. To other work. And that's independent of the status the ticket has. What you bill,whether you bill it completely, half, you can see directly on the object every single time. And that way it's no problem to bill work only partially or reopen it later. That's how I started, but then more and more features were added to the project.

And honestly, I can't work with a normal classic ticket system anymore, but what I've built now, it is software that has tickets, but it also has all the transcripts from the meetings, has all the notes, has all the documentation, has all the people with contact info, and you have an AI that you can ask across all these things. There's a built-in AI already, but you can also choose your own AI, you can also turn the AI off if you want, and you can also run the whole thing locally with your own AI if you want.

Stack: Rails, a single PostgreSQL (with pgvector), Hotwire. AGPL-3.0. Self-host with Docker Compose, or use the hosted version in Germany.

Repo: https://github.com/lalabase/lalabase Site: https://lalabase.com/en

story_text.value:
TL;DR: building a basic AI detector is easy, building one that works is difficult. we realised the need for an adversarial testing pipeline that constantly tests our detector with new patterns, and retrains adapter heads to guard against fresh humanizer patterns.

At first when we built t9xt.com, we trained our model to detect output from frontier models + popular open-source models. We used over 10m text samples from a variety of contexts and writing styles. We hit nearly 100% accuracy on OOF data really fast. But something didn’t seem right - it started bothering us, surely it couldn’t be that easy? and it wasn’t…

The more we tested our model on the raw web, the more it humbled us. Turns out we missed an entire category of text - humanized text. Now I’m sure most of you already know what that is - obscured AI text using techniques like substitution, elongation and superimposition. Often marketed as “beautifying writing”, it doesn’t sound like human writing (to humans) but most AI detectors failed here. So we went in to “crisis mode” and started generating and adding samples from all the humanizers we found, suddenly the water was muddy and the model accuracy nosedived to less than a coin toss ~ 45%. Something was definitely wrong. We had to redesign our model - took months of tinkering but we finally went back above 98% on OOF data (this deserves a separate post so I will spare you the details here). It was great, until it wasn’t - a few weeks later we got sent a sample by one of our early users, and sure enough this humanizer came back as human - and funny enough, the writing didn’t make sense when you read it - jumbled up prose and idiosyncratic text arrangement, it was novel and it hit the mark. When I asked chat to tell me what it meant, and it actually understood it really well - which got me thinking, maybe the writing was not meant for humans in the first place… and the best customers for humanizers, are probably SEO blog SaaS providers that want 500k words to push up their aggregate text on search engines.

A fresh search found over 30 new humanizers, where a few of them still came back as human. This seemed like a never ending loop (we added more data and retrained our model) - then it hit me, why wait for new humanizers? why not just build your own? So I started working on building humanizers for our training data…

The first one we managed to build, got past 60% of the time and the next one 30% - but more importantly we had found an automated way to generate new humanizers. We isolated 20 key base conjugations, wrote an orchestration script (when I say we I meant ChatGPT & I) that bounced off the output against our model in perpetuity studying probabilities and tweaking the pattern mix. We managed to identify 5 unique pattern pipes that went through 40-60% of the time. I was curious so I ran the output against most leading models - and surely enough, it came back as human/likely human over 50% of the time. Some models almost always got it back as human, while others that use a similar training technique to us - flagged it accurately only ~ 50% (which includes part of the text being flagged as human).

Not only did this exercise validate our hypothesis, it also helped emphasise the importance of finding new patterns that might slip through. As a result, we now do this supervised exercise every week and retrain attention heads if accuracy drops more than 3% on any given pattern.

The model of the story: don’t just build, constantly iterate slightly ahead of the curve.

Taken from: t9xt.substack.com/p/how-we-ended-up-building-a-set-of

story_text.value:
There are a lot of fantastic projects posted here. So I thought, why not share something simple and completely pointless for a change?

I've been wanting to build a small, silly side project for a while. Something simple, fun, and not necessarily meant to solve an actual problem.

So I built Hallucination as a Service (HaaS).

The idea is pretty straightforward: an API that returns random excuses for when AI fails to complete a task.

It's obviously a satirical take on all the AI hype we've been hearing lately.

AI is a useful tool, but it's not magic. And sometimes, things just don't work.

Base endpoint:

https://haas.antoniorodriguez.no/hallucination

Source code with use examples:

https://github.com/antoniorodr/hallucination-as-a-service

Built as a small project for fun. Feedback, suggestions, and contributions are welcome!

PS: Only the `excuses.json` is AI generated. The project is written by me.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm a solo founder. Teams building AI agents in a specific domain (legal, healthcare, etc.) have to piece together customer, product and market signals to decide which features to build next for their agent.

This prototype is a product management tool that automates that manual process for PMs and helps them manage the agentic product. It currently runs on sample data (a fictional loans and insurance company).

I'm about to start the MVP, and I'd love feedback from AI agent builders and PMs. In particular: how do you decide what to build today, and what would v1 need to do for you to try it?

title.value: Show HN: Prototype of a product management tool for AI agent companies
